rows.section: Abstract
rows.context: Binary outcomes measured repeatedly on few subjects are analysed with generalized estimating equations (GEE), mixed models or marginalized multilevel models.

rows.section: Abstract
rows.context: Small-sample corrections to the sandwich variance have been evaluated mainly by number of clusters, rarely by number of occasions.

rows.section: Abstract
rows.context: We compared analysis strategies over 2,376 simulated design points (10-145 clusters, 2-10 occasions, four mechanisms, one purely serial) and in subsamples of two clinical datasets.

rows.section: Abstract
rows.context: GEE with a first-order autoregressive working correlation, the Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference, and the marginalized multilevel model with a convergence check and a t reference, were never clearly above 7.5% type I error at any design point and returned a usable result in 92% and 91% of datasets.

rows.section: Abstract
rows.context: Their calibration differed materially only at ten clusters, where GEE was closer to nominal.

rows.section: Abstract
rows.context: The mixed-model Wald test was anticonservative under the Laplace approximation; with adaptive quadrature its excess remained only with ten occasions.

rows.section: Abstract
rows.context: With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters both strategies answered in fewer than half of datasets; a sign-flip score test answered in 72% and kept its level, but gives no estimate.

rows.section: Abstract
rows.context: We recommend the GEE strategy, which needs no convergence check; the marginalized model is a comparable alternative.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: Two strategies met the rule of Section 2.6: GEE with an AR(1) working correlation, the Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference with N - p degrees of freedom; and the marginalized model with the convergence check and a t reference (Figure 1).

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: Across the 2,376 design points of the four mechanisms neither was ever clearly above 7.5%, and they returned a usable result in 92% and 91% of datasets.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: The rule selects the GEE strategy by usable share, but the difference is within the margin.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: In the direct comparison, which was not pre-specified, the two had similar level, usable share and power over the design as a whole.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: We place the GEE strategy first for two reasons: where the two differed beyond the margin, at ten clusters, it was the one closer to nominal, and it needs no convergence check.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: With two occasions and 15 or more clusters the two are comparable; there the GEE strategy is conservative and returns a usable result more often.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: Because the fourth mechanism has AR(1) dependence on the latent scale, it could favour the AR(1) working correlation.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: The working correlation changed the level of Fay-Graubard by less than half a point on average, and the rule selected the same strategy on the three study mechanisms alone (Table S26).

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: The rule asks that a recommendation hold at every design point, because an analyst knows the number of clusters and occasions but not the mechanism that generated the data.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: It replaces a criterion that maximized unconditional validity at each cluster count.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: That criterion rewards a method for answering, whatever its level.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: On the present data it would have recommended the likelihood-ratio test of the mixed model up to 25 clusters, a test that was clearly above 7.5% at 412 design points.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: Fay-Graubard with an exchangeable working correlation would not have met the rule: with a t reference it was clearly above 7.5% at 11 design points, 4 in scenarios M6-M7 and 7 on the fourth mechanism (Table 4).

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters, no strategy with an interval was both available and calibrated.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: The recommended strategy and the marginalized model returned a usable result in fewer than half of the datasets and detected the simulated effect in fewer than 2% of attempted datasets.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: The sign-flip test answered in 72% of those datasets and kept its level, but it detected the simulated effect in only 4.2% of attempted datasets: it gives a valid test where the estimators return nothing, not a powerful one.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: Inverting it gives an interval with nominal coverage (95% under the alternative, against 96% for the GEE strategy, and its non-coverage never clearly outside Bradley's limits at any design point), but in those designs both of its ends were finite in only 14% of datasets, and over all design points, where both intervals existed, it was 17% wider than the GEE interval on average (Section S7).

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: We therefore do not propose it as an interval to use.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: With a random slope and two occasions, the random-effects covariance of the mixed model is not identifiable, since two subject-level parameters saturate two observations, and its Wald test was essentially never usable.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: The case for the maximal random-effects structure [29] is thus bounded by power [30] and, with two occasions, by identifiability.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: In these designs, what can be learned depends more on the number of occasions and clusters than on the analysis.

rows.section: 4.1 The recommendation
rows.context: Four or more occasions per subject, or more clusters, should be planned where possible.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: The check addresses a property of the parametrization rather than of the marginalized model. `MMLB::mm` writes the latent standard deviation with an exponentiated slope, so a slope near zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space, and in scenarios M3-M5 the generating slope was close to zero.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: At the boundary `nlm` either stopped without converging, with an estimate shifted by an amount that did not shrink with the standard error, or converged with a collapsed standard error.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: Both failures produced excess rejections that grew with the number of occasions.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: This is why, without the check, the marginalized model appears miscalibrated with long series.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: Replacing such fits with the fit without the time trend removed the excess.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: The check intervened in a large share of fits (Section 3.2), mainly because `nlm` failed to converge with two or three occasions.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: Where it intervened, the type I error stayed close to nominal.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: It also remained calibrated in M6-M7, where the fit without the time trend is misspecified.

rows.section: 4.2 The convergence check
rows.context: Analysts who use the marginalized model with a latent standard deviation that changes over time should apply the check and report how often it intervened.

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: We reproduce the anticonservatism of the uncorrected sandwich with few clusters [8,9].

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: Li and Redden found that Kauermann-Carroll attains the nominal level at ten clusters under a t reference [16].

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: In our data, with the correction computed from its published formula, its rate at ten clusters under a t reference was 9.1% to 12%, above Bradley's limit, and over the four mechanisms it was clearly above 7.5% at 132 to 199 of 2,376 design points across working correlations.

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: Their clusters were groups of participants [16], whereas ours are subjects measured on several occasions, so the difference may reflect the structure of the clusters rather than the estimator.

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: Our Kauermann-Carroll values come from `fewclust`, which agreed with a computation by hand (Section S4); `geesmv` computes a different quantity, so published values obtained with it are not directly comparable with ours.

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: Mancl and DeRouen reported sizes close to nominal with ten subjects [8], and Bie et al. favoured GEE with the Mancl-DeRouen correction [18].

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: Under a t reference its pooled rate here was 4.7% to 5.3%, inside Bradley's limits.

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: With exchangeable working correlation it was nevertheless clearly above 7.5% at 57 design points, 17 of them in scenarios M6-M7 and 26 on the fourth mechanism.

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: The marginalized model has been studied for moderate to long series [22], and the short series studied here complement that work.

rows.section: 4.3 Relation to previous work
rows.context: Estimation methods for mixed logistic models with few clusters are reviewed by McNeish [31].

rows.section: 4.4 The clinical applications and the fourth mechanism
rows.context: In the neonatal cohort the standard error of the mixed model fell short of the spread of its estimates at every subsample size, and that of the marginalized model was closer to it (Section 3.11).

rows.section: 4.4 The clinical applications and the fourth mechanism
rows.context: In the respiratory trial both fell short with few patients, the marginalized model more than the mixed model up to 15 patients (Table S30).

rows.section: 4.4 The clinical applications and the fourth mechanism
rows.context: With seven mean-model coefficients and few patients its estimates are unstable, and their spread is inflated by large estimates that the usability filter keeps.

rows.section: 4.4 The clinical applications and the fourth mechanism
rows.context: On the fourth mechanism with ten occasions, the excess rejection of the mixed model persisted under adaptive quadrature and comes from its standard error, which ignores the stronger correlation between neighbouring occasions.

rows.section: 4.4 The clinical applications and the fourth mechanism
rows.context: Elsewhere much of its excess came from the Laplace approximation, which is inaccurate with few binary observations per cluster [31].

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: In the main scenarios the random-slope variance and the time trend of the latent standard deviation were small.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: Conclusions about random slopes therefore rest mainly on scenarios M6-M7, which cover one structure (a slope on time) and two mechanisms.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: Trends of the latent standard deviation between those of the main scenarios (0.01 per occasion) and of M6 (0.1) were not simulated; reporting how often the check intervenes (Section 4.2) is the safeguard.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The number of occasions observed did not depend on the outcomes, so informative dropout was not studied, and the results concern a linear treatment-by-time interaction.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: Three working correlations were compared; a misspecified variance function was not simulated.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: Three of the four mechanisms contain a component that is constant within subject, and two of them are the home models of the marginalized model and of the mixed model.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The fourth has only serial dependence, AR(1) on the latent scale, like the working correlation of the GEE strategy; the rule selected the same strategy without it.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: In GLMM-native the marginal value under the null is not exactly zero.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The excess rejection it can cause is at most 0.029 percentage points in the main scenarios and 0.26 in M6-M7 for the marginalized model and the GEEs, and subtracting it changes none of the flags clearly above 7.5% or clearly below 2.5% of these methods.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The convergence check was introduced after part of the results had been seen, and was then tested on scenarios simulated afterwards.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The decision rule itself replaced the criterion of an earlier version after that version's results had been seen, and the direct comparison of the two strategies that met the rule was not pre-specified.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The tables report the mixed model fitted by the Laplace approximation, the default of `lme4`; adaptive quadrature, which `lme4` offers only with a single random intercept, was examined after the main run on a subset of design points (Section 3.10) and could not be examined with random slopes [31].

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: Penalized GEE [15] and the degrees of freedom proposed with the Fay-Graubard correction [10] were not evaluated.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: Treatment was assigned by simple randomization with probability one half, so with ten subjects some datasets had unbalanced arms, and datasets with a degenerate design were excluded.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: Mancl-DeRouen and Fay-Graubard were computed with two implementations that agreed; the Kauermann-Carroll results rest on one.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The sign-flip test gives no estimate, and its interval is rarely bounded where it would be most needed.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The clinical applications use two datasets with one outcome each.

rows.section: 4.5 Limitations
rows.context: The subsampling resamples whole patients, and in the neonatal cohort the patient-timepoint level that carries most of the dependence is identified by only 22 patients measured more than once.

rows.section: 5. Conclusions
rows.context: With few clusters and short series, the choice of analysis for a clustered binary outcome decides whether the test keeps its nominal level and whether it returns an answer at all.

rows.section: 5. Conclusions
rows.context: GEE with an AR(1) working correlation, the Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference, and the marginalized multilevel model fitted with a convergence check and a t reference, were never clearly above 7.5% at any simulated design point of four mechanisms, and their calibration differed beyond the relevance margin only at ten clusters.

rows.section: 5. Conclusions
rows.context: The Wald test of the mixed model fitted by the Laplace approximation was anticonservative; with adaptive quadrature, examined for a random intercept, the excess remained only with ten occasions, mainly under serial dependence, and with few clusters the test became conservative.

rows.section: 5. Conclusions
rows.context: With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters, neither strategy returned a usable result in half of the datasets.

rows.section: 5. Conclusions
rows.context: A sign-flip score test can still test for an effect there, with little power, and no analysis estimates the effect reliably; in that regime the design limits what any analysis can show.

rows.section: 5. Conclusions
rows.context: In the designs studied we recommend GEE with an AR(1) working correlation, the Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference with N - p degrees of freedom, which needs no convergence check and was closer to nominal at ten clusters.

rows.section: 5. Conclusions
rows.context: The marginalized model with the convergence check and a t reference is a competitive alternative, slightly closer to nominal with two occasions and 15 or more clusters.
